input.step_by_step_reasoning: The whiteboard shows 8 entities, all kept as separate nodes (no fusion or expansion needed): satellite source, EC2 Spot, S3, RDS, ElastiCache, Fargate, Lambda and the web users. The Lambda icon is described as a series of Lambda functions acting as one logical unit, so it stays a single node. Three flows come from the transcript. Flow 0 (ingestion): satellite tiles arrive at an EC2 Spot cluster, which post-processes them and stores bulk data in S3 and metadata in RDS; the ledger's reverse arrows S3->EC2 and RDS->EC2 are not described in the audio and are emitted as data edges with empty notes. Flow 1 (map tile serving): the user requests tiles from Fargate, which checks the Redis cache in ElastiCache, looks up source imagery in RDS, reads partial objects from S3 with HTTP range requests, stitches/downsamples/colour-corrects, writes to cache and returns the tile. Flow 2 (time-series analytics): the farmer's area of interest is passed to Lambda, which looks up imagery in RDS, reads from S3, clips and summarises, and returns the time series. Self-check: visual_connections has 19 entries and I emit 19 edges, one per entry with the same source and target; no edges were added beyond the ledger.

graph.name: Indigo Carbon: Serverless Satellite Imagery Processing for Regenerative Agriculture
graph.notes: Indigo Carbon ingests satellite imagery (e.g. from NASA) with EC2 Spot clusters, stores bulk data in S3 and metadata in RDS, serves map web tiles on the fly from Fargate with a Redis cache in ElastiCache, and computes per-field time series with Lambda functions. Catalogue spans about 30 years (mostly the last 10), about 5 PB in total, growing about 100 GB per day. On-the-fly processing saves orders of magnitude of cost.

nodes.name: Satellite
nodes.notes: Existing satellites from organizations such as NASA. Delivers a series of modestly processed and corrected imagery tiles throughout each day.

nodes.name: EC2 Spot
nodes.notes: Large cluster of Spot instances spun up as quickly as possible to post-process incoming imagery (further correction and conversion to more accessible formats), then spun back down.

nodes.name: S3
nodes.notes: Stores the bulk imagery data as relatively large compressed chunks. About 5 PB in total, catalogue spanning about 30 years (mostly the last 10), growing about 100 GB per day. Read partially using HTTP range requests.

nodes.name: RDS
nodes.notes: Stores imagery metadata; used to look up which source imagery corresponds to a tile or area of interest.

nodes.name: AWS Fargate
nodes.notes: Cluster serving map web tiles. A map load is sliced into about 16 tiles, each an individual request. Stitches image parts together, downsamples to the right resolution, then applies colour correction (RGB) or colour mapping (intensity values) on the fly.

nodes.name: ElastiCache
nodes.notes: Redis used as a central cache for already generated tiles. Common tiles (such as the whole-US view) are computed once and then served from cache.

nodes.name: Lambda
nodes.notes: Series of Lambda functions that compute a time series from the source data cube: build the tile of interest, clip it to the farmer's custom field area, compute a summary (e.g. mean greenness), repeated about 1000 times.

nodes.name: Users
nodes.notes: Farmers using the web app: view a map of the United States with the most up-to-date imagery, select layer and time frame, and supply their field boundaries.
